definitions.explanation: A style of writing that uses modern spoken Japanese grammar and vocabulary, as opposed to the classical literary style ({文語体|ぶんごたい}). In Japanese linguistics, this refers specifically to the modern language style that became standard after the Meiji-era language reforms.

examples.japanese: この{小説|しょうせつ}は{口語体|こうごたい}で{書|か}かれている。
examples.english: This novel is written in colloquial style.

examples.japanese: {明治|めいじ}{時代|じだい}に{口語体|こうごたい}の{文学|ぶんがく}が{広|ひろ}まった。
examples.english: Literature in the colloquial style spread during the Meiji period.

examples.japanese: {口語体|こうごたい}と{文語体|ぶんごたい}の{違|ちが}いを{理解|りかい}することは、{日本語|にほんご}の{歴史|れきし}を{学|まな}ぶ{上|うえ}で{重要|じゅうよう}だ。
examples.english: Understanding the difference between colloquial and literary styles is important for studying the history of Japanese.

notes:
Composed of {口語|こうご} (spoken language) + {体|たい} (style/form). This is a key term in Japanese linguistics and literary history, referring to the writing style based on modern spoken Japanese.

ETYMOLOGY:
Before the Meiji period, written Japanese ({文語体|ぶんごたい}) was very different from spoken Japanese. The {言文一致|げんぶんいっち} (unification of speech and writing) movement in the late 19th century promoted writing in the same style as speech, leading to the dominance of {口語体|こうごたい} in modern Japanese.

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- {口語体|こうごたい}で{書|か}く: to write in colloquial style
- {口語体|こうごたい}の{文章|ぶんしょう}: colloquial-style writing
- {口語体|こうごたい}と{文語体|ぶんごたい}: colloquial and literary styles

SIMILAR WORDS:
- {文語体|ぶんごたい}: literary/classical style — the contrasting style based on classical Japanese grammar
- {口語|こうご}: spoken language — the language itself, not the writing style
- {話し言葉|はなしことば}: spoken language — more everyday term, less technical
